Stable Quadratic Polynomials over ℚ⁡(i)\mathbb{Q}(i)

Jermain McDermott
Abstract.

We study iterates of a quadratic f=x2+1/c∈K⁡[x]f=x^{2}+1/c\in K[x]. If the number of factors of fn:=f∘f∘…∘ff^{n}:=f\circ f\circ...\circ f is bounded by a constant independent of nn, then ff is said to be eventually stable. This paper is an extension to ℚ⁡(i)\mathbb{Q}(i) of the paper [6], which considered ff over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. The conjecture "if f2f^{2} is irreducible, then fnf^{n} is irreducible for all nn" extends to ℚ⁡(i)\mathbb{Q}(i), but the lack of a linear ordering on ℚ⁡(i)\mathbb{Q}(i) requires us to pass to the norm. As a result, an auxiliary function is necessary for a lower bound on a finite nn to check. The elusive case of c≡2mod4c\equiv 2\bmod 4 (as a ℤ\mathbb{Z} equivalence class) is shown to be "stable" over ℚ⁡(i)\mathbb{Q}(i), offering more evidence for [6, Conjecture 1]. Stability for c≡1mod2c\equiv 1\bmod 2 (as a ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i] equivalence class) is not as fully handled as over ℤ\mathbb{Z}, however.

1. Introduction

Suppose KK is a field with algebraic closure K¯\overline{K}. Let f⁡(x)=x2+r∈K⁡[x]f(x)=x^{2}+r\in K[x], and denote its iterates by

fn​(x):=(f∘f∘…∘f)​(x)​ (n compositions)  with ​f0​(x)=x.f^{n}(x):=(f\circ f\circ...\circ f)(x)\text{ ($n$ compositions) }\quad\text{ with }f^{0}(x)=x.

Fix α∈K\alpha\in K and denote by f−n​(α):={β∈K¯:fn​(β)=α}.f^{-n}(\alpha):=\{\beta\in\overline{K}:f^{n}(\beta)=\alpha\}. If fn​(x)−αf^{n}(x)-\alpha is separable, the disjoint union Tf,∞​(α):={α}⊔f−1​(α)⊔f−2​(α)⊔⋯T_{f,\infty}(\alpha):=\{\alpha\}\sqcup f^{-1}(\alpha)\sqcup f^{-2}(\alpha)\sqcup\cdots is a rooted tree with root vertex α\alpha, and edges assigned according to the action of ff. Denote by Aut​(Tf​(α))\text{Aut}(T_{f}(\alpha)) the tree automorphisms of Tf​(α)T_{f}(\alpha). Since the natural action of the Galois group GK:=Gal​(K¯/K)G_{K}:=\text{Gal}(\overline{K}/K) on f−n​(α)f^{-n}(\alpha) commutes with f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x], we obtain a homomorphism Gal​(K¯/K)→Aut​(Tf​(α))\text{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)\to\text{Aut}(T_{f}(\alpha)) called the arboreal Galois representation associated to (f,α)(f,\alpha). One of the central problems in arithmetic dynamics is whether the image of this homomorphism has finite index in Aut​(Tf​(α))\text{Aut}(T_{f}(\alpha)); a dynamical parallel of the Serre open image theorem. This question has generated a large literature, see [1] for a summary of this and other current research in the field.

In this article, we attempt to characterize factorizations of fn​(x)−αf^{n}(x)-\alpha for α=0\alpha=0.

Definition 1.1.

Let KK be a field, f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x], and α∈K\alpha\in K. For n≥1n\geq 1 let knk_{n} denote the number of irreducible factors of fn​(x)−αf^{n}(x)-\alpha over KK. We call the pair (f,α)(f,\alpha) (resp. ff) eventually stable over KK if there is a constant C⁡(f,α)C(f,\alpha) (resp. C⁡(f,0)C(f,0)) such that for all nn,

kn≤C⁡(f,α).k_{n}\leq C(f,\alpha).

The pair (f,α)(f,\alpha) is called stable over KK if C⁡(f,α)=1C(f,\alpha)=1, i.e. fn​(x)−αf^{n}(x)-\alpha is irreducible over KK for all n≥1n\geq 1.

Eventual stability is applied in some finite-index results for certain arboreal Galois representations [3, 4], and is equivalent to a bound independent of nn on the number of Galois orbits on f−n​(α)f^{-n}(\alpha) [8, Proposition 2.2]. However, this is a straightforward consequence of the image of the arboreal representation associated to (f,α)(f,\alpha) having finite index, so finite index of the arboreal representation implies eventual stability. The reverse implication is much less clear. Other applications include finiteness of SS-integer points in backwards orbits; see [8, Section 3] for a discussion of these and other results concerning the topic.

The following theorem of Hamblen, Jones, and Madhu [7] establishes eventual stability of a large class of polynomials over number fields (using ideas resembling Eisenstein’s criterion):

Theorem 1.2.

(Hamblen, Jones and Madhu, [7, Theorem 5]) Let d≥2d\geq 2, let KK be a field of characteristic not dividing dd, and let f⁡(x)=xd+r∈K⁡[x]f(x)=x^{d}+r\in K[x]. If there is a discrete non-archimedean absolute value on KK with |r|<1|r|<1, then ff is eventually stable over KK.

The following corollary is an extension of [7, Corollary 6] considered by DeMark et al.:

Corollary 1.3.

Let f⁡(x)=xd+r∈ℚ⁡(i)​[x]f(x)=x^{d}+r\in\mathbb{Q}(i)[x], and suppose that rr is non-zero and is not the reciprocal of an element of ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i]. Then ff is eventually stable over ℚ⁡(i)\mathbb{Q}(i).

This paper is concerned with the case when d=2d=2 and a non-zero r≠−1r\neq-1 is a reciprocal of an element of ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i]. In this case, "Eisenstein-type" methods break down. The following conjecture attempts to fully describe the situation. It is an extension of [6, Conjecture 1.7] which considered r∈ℚr\in\mathbb{Q}, but negatives have turned into squares, while the cc-factorization 4​m2​(m2−1)4m^{2}(m^{2}-1) for f2−f^{2}-reducibility over ℤ\mathbb{Z} expands to c=α2​(2​i−α2)c=\alpha^{2}(2i-\alpha^{2}):

Conjecture 1.4.

Let fr=x2+rf_{r}=x^{2}+r with r=1/cr=1/c for c∈ℤ⁡[i]\{0,−1}c\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\backslash\{0,-1\}, and let knk_{n} denote the number of irreducible factors of frn​(x)f_{r}^{n}(x). Then frf_{r} is eventually stable over ℚ⁡(i)\mathbb{Q}(i) with constant C⁡(fr,0)=4C(f_{r},0)=4:

  1. (1)

    If c=α2c=\alpha^{2} with 1±i​α∈ℤ⁡[i]\ℤ​[i]21\pm i\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\backslash\mathbb{Z}[i]^{2} then kn=2k_{n}=2 for all n≥1n\geq 1.

  2. (2)

    If c∈{±8​i,−16}⊂ℤ​[i]2c\in\{\pm 8i,-16\}\subset\mathbb{Z}[i]^{2}, then k1=k2=2k_{1}=k_{2}=2, kn=3k_{n}=3 for all n≥3n\geq 3.

  3. (3)

    If c=(i​σ2−i)2c=(i\sigma^{2}-i)^{2} for ±σ∈ℤ⁡[i]\{3,5,56}\pm\sigma\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\backslash\{3,5,56\} then k1=2k_{1}=2 and kn=3k_{n}=3 for all n≥2n\geq 2.

  4. (4)

    If c=(i​s2−i)2c=(is^{2}-i)^{2} for ±s∈{3,5,56}\pm s\in\{3,5,56\} then k1=2k_{1}=2, k2=3k_{2}=3 and kn=4k_{n}=4 for all n≥3n\geq 3.

  5. (5)

    If c≠48c\neq 48 and c=α2​(2​i−α2)c=\alpha^{2}(2i-\alpha^{2}) for some α∈ℤ⁡[i]\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}[i], then k1=1k_{1}=1 and kn=2k_{n}=2 for all n≥2n\geq 2.

  6. (6)

    If c=48c=48, then k1=1,k2=2k_{1}=1,k_{2}=2, and kn=3k_{n}=3 for all n≥3n\geq 3.

  7. (7)

    If c∈ℤ⁡[i]\ℤ​[i]2c\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\backslash\mathbb{Z}[i]^{2} and c≠α2​(2​i−α2)c\neq\alpha^{2}(2i-\alpha^{2}) for any α∈ℤ⁡[i]\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}[i] (i.e. cc is not in an above case), then kn=1k_{n}=1 for all n≥1n\geq 1.

All irreducibility statements from here on will be over the field KK, and r=1/cr=1/c where c∈ℤ⁡[i]c\in\mathbb{Z}[i]. Case (3) and (4) are where c=α2c=\alpha^{2} with 1±i​α∈ℤ​[i]21\pm i\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}[i]^{2}. Case (7) is precisely the case where fr2​(x)f^{2}_{r}(x) is irreducible and thus case (7) asserts that if fr2​(x)f^{2}_{r}(x) is irreducible, then frn​(x)f^{n}_{r}(x) is irreducible for all n≥1n\geq 1. This is the main focus of this paper, and we state this as a ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i] analogue of [6, Conjecture 1.8]:

Conjecture 1.5.

Let fr​(x)=x2+rf_{r}(x)=x^{2}+r with r=1/cr=1/c for c∈ℤ⁡[i]\{0,−1}c\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\backslash\{0,-1\}. If fr2​(x)f^{2}_{r}(x) is irreducible over KK, then ff is stable over KK.

The determination of squares in the sequence {frn​(0)}\{f_{r}^{n}(0)\} is of central importance in this study. To this end, we use tools such as the non-linear recurrence relation

a1=1,an​(c)=c2n−1−1+an−12​(c)for ​n≥2a_{1}=1,\quad a_{n}(c)=c^{2^{n-1}-1}+a_{n-1}^{2}(c)\quad\text{for }n\geq 2

describing the numerator of frn​(0)=anc2n−1f_{r}^{n}(0)=\frac{a_{n}}{c^{2^{n-1}}} for n≥1n\geq 1 (note c2n−1c^{2^{n-1}} is a square when n≥2n\geq 2).

We prove another irreducibility test involving the ana_{n} sequence.

Lemma 1.6.

Suppose that c∈ℤ⁡[i]\{0}c\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\backslash\{0\}, r=1/cr=1/c and fr2f_{r}^{2} is irreducible. Let an=an​(c)a_{n}=a_{n}(c) be defined as above and set

(1) bn±​(c)=i⁡(an−1±an)∈ℚ¯.b_{n}^{\pm}(c)=i(a_{n-1}\pm\sqrt{a_{n}})\in\bar{\mathbb{Q}}.

If bn±​(c)b_{n}^{\pm}(c) is not a square in ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i] (which holds in particular if an​(c)a_{n}(c) is non-square in ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i]) for all n≥3n\geq 3, then frn​(x)f_{r}^{n}(x) is irreducible for all n≥1n\geq 1.

It is a ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i] analogue of [6, Lemma 1.10], but the lack of a linear ordering on ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i] requires that we check that bn−b_{n}^{-} is non-square as well. This leads us to the following ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i] extension of [6, Conjecture 1.11]:

Conjecture 1.7.

Let bn±​(c)b_{n}^{\pm}(c) be defined as in 1. If c∈ℤ⁡[i]\{0,−1}c\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\backslash\{0,-1\}, then bn±​(c)b_{n}^{\pm}(c) is non-square in ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i] for all n≥3n\geq 3.

The {bn±​(c)}\{b_{n}^{\pm}(c)\} square test of Lemma 1.6 allows us to prove a ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i] analogue of [6, Theorem 1.3]. This theorem is in some ways weaker than its counterpart in [6] due to the lack of linear ordering on ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i], however, it also expands on that theorem:

Theorem 1.8.

Let fr​(x)=x2+rf_{r}(x)=x^{2}+r with r=1/cr=1/c. Then frnf_{r}^{n} is irreducible for all n≥1n\geq 1 if cc satisfies one of the following conditions:

  1. (1)

    c,c+1∈ℤ⁡[i]\ℤ​[i]2c,c+1\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\backslash\mathbb{Z}[i]^{2}, 2∤c2\nmid c and 16∤c+116\nmid c+1;

  2. (2)

    c+1∈ℤ⁡[i]\ℤ​[i]2c+1\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\backslash\mathbb{Z}[i]^{2}, and c≡±imoda+b​ic\equiv\pm i\bmod a+bi with N⁡(a+b​i)≡5mod8N(a+bi)\equiv 5\mod 8

  3. (3)

    c∈ℤ⁡[i]\{0,−1,−1±2​i}c\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\backslash\{0,-1,-1\pm 2i\} and vπ​(c)v_{\pi}(c) is odd for all primes π|c\pi\mid c.

A notable consequence of item (2) is that for integers c≡2mod4c\equiv 2\mod 4, frf_{r} is stable over ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i] (and therefore ℤ\mathbb{Z}). Thus, by [6, Corollary 4.6], c≢0mod4c\not\equiv 0\mod 4 implies frf_{r} is stable over ℤ\mathbb{Z} (when cc is non-square in ℤ\mathbb{Z}).

We prove another result allowing us to check irreducibility of fkf^{k} for some finite kk to determine stability of ff. The lack of a linear ordering on ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i] leads to a new function Ξ⁡(c)\Xi(c) for our bound, rather than ϵ⁡(c)\epsilon(c) of [6, Theorem 1.4]. This also leads to a smaller denominator log⁡1+1|c|<log⁡(1+1|c|)\log\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{|c|}}<\log(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{|c|}}):

Theorem 1.9.

Let fr​(x)=x2+rf_{r}(x)=x^{2}+r with r=1/cr=1/c for c∈ℤ⁡[i]c\in\mathbb{Z}[i] with |c|≥5|c|\geq 5. If fkf^{k} is irreducible for

k=1+⌊log2⁡(1+log⁡4+Ξ⁡(|c|)/|c|log⁡1+1/|c|)⌋,k=1+\left\lfloor\log_{2}\left(1+\frac{\log{4}+\Xi(|c|)/\sqrt{|c|}}{\log{\sqrt{1+1/|c|}}}\right)\right\rfloor,

then all fnf^{n} are irreducible. Here Ξ⁡(|c|)\Xi(|c|) is a monotonically decreasing function on ℝ≥5\mathbb{R}_{\geq 5} with

2<Ξ⁡(|c|)≤Ξ⁡(5)<6.05​(see Definition 4.6)\sqrt{2}<\Xi(|c|)\leq\Xi(5)<6.05\text{(see \lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{def4.5})}

Now, we define the orbit of t∈ℚ⁡(i)t\in\mathbb{Q}(i) under frf_{r} to be the set Ofr​(t)={t,fr​(t),fr2​(t),…}O_{f_{r}}(t)=\{t,f_{r}(t),f_{r}^{2}(t),...\}, and we say that a prime π\pi divides Ofr​(t)O_{f_{r}}(t) if there is at least one nonzero α∈Ofr​(t)\alpha\in O_{f_{r}}(t) with vπ​(α)>0v_{\pi}(\alpha)>0. We prove the following ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i] analogue of [6, Proposition 6.1], showing that the natural density of prime divisors of orbits is 0 when bn±b_{n}^{\pm} is non-square for all n≥3n\geq 3. The difficulty in a proof of this over ℚ⁡(i)\mathbb{Q}(i) is constructing the correct tower of Galois extensions on which to apply Chebotarev’s theorem:

Theorem 1.10.

Let fr​(x)=x2+rf_{r}(x)=x^{2}+r for r=1/cr=1/c for c∈ℤ⁡[i]\{0,−1}c\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\backslash\{0,-1\}, with c,c+1c,c+1 both non-square in ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i]. If {|bn+|2,|bn−|2}\{|b_{n}^{+}|^{2},|b_{n}^{-}|^{2}\} contains no squares in ℤ\mathbb{Z} for all n≥3n\geq 3, then for any t∈ℚ⁡(i)t\in\mathbb{Q}(i) we have

D⁡({π​ prime in ​ℤ​[i]:π​ divides ​Ofr​(t)})=0.D(\{\pi\text{ prime in }\mathbb{Z}[i]:\pi\text{ divides }O_{f_{r}}(t)\})=0.

2. Background

We first list some work-saving facts:

Proposition 2.1.

If p​(x)∈ℚ​(i)​[x]p(x)\in\mathbb{Q}(i)[x], then any factorization of pp into irreducible polynomials over ℚ⁡(i)\mathbb{Q}(i) has the same number of factors as p¯​(x)\bar{p}(x), p⁡(x)p(x) with conjugated coefficients. In particular, the polynomial frn​(x)f^{n}_{r}(x) has the same number of factors irreducible over ℚ⁡(i)\mathbb{Q}(i) as fr¯n​(x)f^{n}_{\bar{r}}(x).

Proof.

Since conjugation is a field automorphism of ℚ⁡(i)\mathbb{Q}(i), it extends to a ring automorphism of ℚ​(i)​[z]\mathbb{Q}(i)[z]. Ring automorphisms preserve irreducibility. ∎

This allows us to only consider cc in quadrants 1 and 3, reducing our work load by "half".

We also will need some way of inferring irreducibility of iterated polynomials: the following (derived from Capelli’s Lemma) translates irreducibility of the list {g⁡(fn​(x))}n≥1\{g(f^{n}(x))\}_{n\geq 1} to a property of a sequence in KK.

Lemma 2.2.

(Demark-Hindes-Jones-Misplon-Stoll-Stoneman, [6, Lemma 2.2]) Let KK be a field with c​h​a​r​(K)≠2char(K)\neq 2, g∈K⁡[x]g\in K[x] a monic, irreducible polynomial with d:=deg⁡(g)≥1d:=\deg(g)\geq 1, and f⁡(x)f(x) monic and quadratic with critical point β\beta. If the set

{(−1)d​g​(f⁡(β))}∪{g⁡(fn​(β))}n≥2\{(-1)^{d}g(f(\beta))\}\cup\{g(f^{n}(\beta))\}_{n\geq 2}

contains no squares in KK, then g​(fn​(x))g(f^{n}(x)) is irreducible over KK for all n≥1n\geq 1.

Remark.

The proof found in [6, Lemma 2.2] shows that if g​(fn​(x))g(f^{n}(x)) is irreducible (over KK) for some n≥1n\geq 1 and g​(fn+1​(β))g(f^{n+1}(\beta)) is non-square in KK, then g​(fn+1​(x))g(f^{n+1}(x)) is irreducible (over KK).

When g⁡(x)=fr​(x)=x2+rg(x)=f_{r}(x)=x^{2}+r, the hypothesis asks if the set {frn(0)=an​(c)c2n−1}n≥1\{f_{r}^{n}(0)=\frac{a_{n}(c)}{c^{2^{n-1}}}\}_{n\geq 1} contains no squares in KK ⇔\iff the set {an=an−12(c)+c2n−1−1}n≥1\{a_{n}=a_{n-1}^{2}(c)+c^{2^{n-1}-1}\}_{n\geq 1} contains no squares in ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i].

This idea that we may infer irreducibility of fnf^{n} by considering whether fn​(0)f^{n}(0) is a square leads to necessary and sufficient conditions for the irreducibility of frf_{r} and fr2f^{2}_{r} when frf_{r} is irreducible. The following specialization is one of the first instances where the lack of ordering changes our results:

Proposition 2.3.

Let fr​(x)=x2+rf_{r}(x)=x^{2}+r with r=1/cr=1/c for c∈ℤ⁡[i]\{0}c\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\backslash\{0\}. Then fr​(x)f_{r}(x) is reducible if and only if c=α2c=\alpha^{2} for some α∈ℤ⁡[i]\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}[i]. If fr​(x)f_{r}(x) is irreducible, then fr2​(x)f^{2}_{r}(x) is reducible if and only if c=α2​(2​i−α2)c=\alpha^{2}(2i-\alpha^{2}) for some α∈ℤ⁡[i]\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}[i].

Proof.

The first statement is clear. Now suppose frf_{r} is irreducible over ℚ⁡(i)\mathbb{Q}(i). If c=α2​(2​i−α2)c=\alpha^{2}(2i-\alpha^{2}), then

fr2​(x)=(x2−1+iα​x−i​α2+1α2​(2​i−α2))​(x2+1+iα​x−i​α2+1α2​(2​i−α2)).f^{2}_{r}(x)=\left(x^{2}-\frac{1+i}{\alpha}x-\frac{i\alpha^{2}+1}{\alpha^{2}(2i-\alpha^{2})}\right)\left(x^{2}+\frac{1+i}{\alpha}x-\frac{i\alpha^{2}+1}{\alpha^{2}(2i-\alpha^{2})}\right).

These factors are reducible if and only if their discriminant −2​iα2−2​i\frac{-2i}{\alpha^{2}-2i} is square in ℚ⁡(i)\mathbb{Q}(i) (i.e. α2−2​i\alpha^{2}-2i is a square in ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i]): suppose α2−2​i=η2\alpha^{2}-2i=\eta^{2}. Then 2​i=(α−η)​(α+η)2i=(\alpha-\eta)(\alpha+\eta). If {α+η,α−η}={−1+i,1−i}\{\alpha+\eta,\alpha-\eta\}=\{-1+i,1-i\}, this implies 2​α=02\alpha=0. Since c≠0c\neq 0, we have a contradiction. We obtain similar contradictions when {α+η,α−η}∈±{{1+i,1+i},{1,2​i},{i,2}}\{\alpha+\eta,\alpha-\eta\}\in\pm\{\{1+i,1+i\},\{1,2i\},\{i,2\}\}. Thus the factors of fr2​(x)f^{2}_{r}(x) are irreducible over ℚ⁡(i)\mathbb{Q}(i) when c=α2​(2​i−α2)c=\alpha^{2}(2i-\alpha^{2}).

The converse is analogous to the proof of [6, Proposition 2.1], but 2​(k2−1)​(−1±k)2(k^{2}-1)(-1\pm k) is potentially a square in ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i] instead of only 2​(k2−1)​(−1+k)2(k^{2}-1)(-1+k) over ℚ\mathbb{Q} (where c=k2−1c=k^{2}-1). We also need to factor 2=i​(1−i)22=i(1-i)^{2}.

∎

Non-squares in K=ℚ⁡(i)K=\mathbb{Q}(i) are thus of great interest, so squares in ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i] are too. A tactic is checking for quadratic non-residues: if the Gaussian integer α\alpha is non-square mod π\pi, then α\alpha is non-square in ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i]. In the rest of this paper, [⋅α]\genfrac{[}{]}{}{}{\cdot}{\alpha} and [⋅π]2\genfrac{[}{]}{}{}{\cdot}{\pi}_{\!2} refer to the Gaussian integer Jacobi and Legendre symbols (respectively) as in [5]. Thus if α=π1a1⋅π2a2⋯πnan\alpha=\pi_{1}^{a_{1}}\cdot\pi_{2}^{a_{2}}\cdots\pi_{n}^{a_{n}} is a prime factorization of α∈ℤ⁡[i]\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}[i], then

[σα]=[σπ1]2a1⋅[σπ2]2a2⋯[σπn]2an=−1 if σ is a non-residue modα.\genfrac{[}{]}{}{}{\sigma}{\alpha}=\genfrac{[}{]}{}{}{\sigma}{\pi_1}_{\!2}^{a_{1}}\cdot\genfrac{[}{]}{}{}{\sigma}{\pi_2}_{\!2}^{a_{2}}\cdots\genfrac{[}{]}{}{}{\sigma}{\pi_n}_{\!2}^{a_{n}}=-1\quad\text{ if }\sigma\text{ is a non-residue }\bmod\alpha.

The notion of a "rigid divisibility sequence" will also be advantageous in this search for non-squares.

2.1. Rigid divisibility

One can show inductively that f1/cn​(0)=an/c2n−1f_{1/c}^{n}(0)=a_{n}/c^{2^{n-1}}, where

a1​(c)=1,an​(c)=an−12​(c)+c2n−1−1 for ​n≥2.a_{1}(c)=1,\quad a_{n}(c)=a^{2}_{n-1}(c)+c^{2^{n-1}-1}\quad\text{ for }n\geq 2.

Note that the numerator ana_{n} is relatively prime to the denominator c2n−1c^{2^{n-1}}, a square when n>1n>1. This numerator inherits prime divisors in a predictable way, leading to the notion of "rigid divisibility":

Definition 2.4.

Let A={zn}n≥1A=\{z_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} be a sequence in a field KK. We say AA is a rigid divisibility sequence over KK if for each non-archimedean absolute value |⋅||\cdot| on KK, the following hold:

(1) if |zn|<1|z_{n}|<1, then |zn|=|zk​n||z_{n}|=|z_{kn}| for any k≥1k\geq 1.

(2) if |zn|<1|z_{n}|<1 and |zj|<1|z_{j}|<1, then |zgcd​(n,j)|<1|z_{\text{gcd}(n,j)}|<1.

The following theorem establishes rigid divisibility of {fn​(0)}n≥1\{f^{n}(0)\}_{n\geq 1}, and implies that the {an}n≥1\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} sequence also has this property:

Theorem 2.5.

(Hamblen, Jones and Madhu, [7, Lemma 12]) Let KK be a field and f⁡(x)=xd+r∈K⁡[x]f(x)=x^{d}+r\in K[x] for some d≥2d\geq 2. Then {fn​(0)}n≥1\{f^{n}(0)\}_{n\geq 1} is a rigid divisibility sequence over KK.

Lemma 3.4.

If c+1∈ℤ⁡[i]\ℤ​[i]2c+1\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\backslash\mathbb{Z}[i]^{2}, and c≡±imoda+b​ic\equiv\pm i\bmod a+bi with N⁡(a+b​i)≡5mod8N(a+bi)\equiv 5\mod 8, then {an}n≥2\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 2} contains no squares in ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i]. Thus frnf_{r}^{n} is irreducible for all n≥1n\geq 1.

4. A useful factorization of cc

We first note the following extension of [6, Lemma 4.1] to the Gaussian integers (where N:ℂ→ℝN:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{R} is the field norm Nℂ/ℝ​(a+i​b)=a2+b2N_{\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{R}}(a+ib)=a^{2}+b^{2}):

d​v2n−1−1−u2n−1−1d=2​an−1​(u​v)dv^{2^{n-1}-1}-\frac{u^{2^{n-1}-1}}{d}=2a_{n-1}(uv)

This is the proof of [6, Lemma 4.1] with minor modifications. The hypothesis that |bn±​(c)|2|b_{n}^{\pm}(c)|^{2} are non-square is strictly weaker than an​(c)a_{n}(c) being non-square for n≥2n\geq 2. When an​(c)a_{n}(c) is non-square for all n≥2n\geq 2, the conclusion follows by (2) of [7, Theorem 1.1].
